analysis.one_liner: Licenses mortgage loan officers, tightens mortgage disclosures and oversight of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and funds housing counseling.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan-cosponsored-in-name-only Republican housing crisis bill with 61 House supporters died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Introduced at the height of the 2008 foreclosure crisis, the bill would have required everyone who arranges home loans to pass background checks, education, and a written test, and to carry a public tracking number showing their disciplinary history. It would have forced lenders to tell borrowers in plain language how high their payments could go, created a federal Office of Housing Counseling, extended foreclosure protections for service members returning from abroad, funded mortgage fraud prosecution, and replaced the weak regulators of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac with a single agency with real enforcement powers.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and borrowers facing foreclosure, who would get clearer loan disclosures, certified housing counseling, and a public database of loan officers' records. Service members, whose foreclosure protections would be extended. Taxpayers, who would gain stronger oversight of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and funding for mortgage fraud prosecution.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Homebuyers, borrowers facing foreclosure, service members

how_it_helps.text: Every mortgage loan originator would need a license or registration, FBI background checks, 20 hours of pre-licensing education, and a passing score of 75% on a 100-question test, with a unique identifier giving the public access to their employment and disciplinary history [S3].

Lenders would have to disclose the maximum possible monthly payment on adjustable loans ('Your payment can go as high as $__'), disclose fees paid to the originator, and send monthly statements showing the balance, rate, and next reset date [S3].

The bill creates an Office of Housing Counseling at HUD and authorizes $45 million per year for fiscal 2009 through 2012 for grants to governments and nonprofits providing homeownership and rental counseling [S3].

It directs the Defense Department to set up foreclosure prevention counseling for service members returning from abroad and extends the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act's protection against mortgage foreclosure [S2][S3].

It abolishes the Office of Federal Housing Enterprise Oversight and the Federal Housing Finance Board and creates the Federal Housing Finance Agency with capital requirements, enforcement powers, and executive compensation authority over Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Home Loan Banks [S2][S3].
It authorizes appropriations for federal prosecution of mortgage fraud and adds appraisal independence requirements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage brokers and independent loan officers, who face licensing, testing, and education costs; Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and the Federal Home Loan Banks, which face a tougher regulator with capital mandates and enforcement power; and lenders generally, who face new disclosure and escrow obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mortgage brokers, lenders, and the GSEs

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a two-tier system: employees of banks and their subsidiaries only register with federal agencies, while independent mortgage brokers must obtain full state licenses with education and testing — a structure that lightens the burden for banks relative to their competitors [S3].

Title IV gives lenders a 'safe harbor' from liability for qualified loan modifications and lets them earn Community Reinvestment Act credit for modifying loans, shielding them from lawsuits rather than mandating relief for borrowers [S3].

The bill offers counseling and disclosure but no direct foreclosure relief — no requirement to modify loans, no aid to homeowners behind on payments — at a moment when foreclosures were surging [S2][S3].
The FHA modernization provisions raise loan limits and expand government-insured lending, shifting more mortgage risk onto federal insurance funds backed by taxpayers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core protections — originator licensing, honest payment-shock disclosures, housing counseling, and a real regulator for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — would have addressed documented causes of the foreclosure wave. Its weaknesses are that it protects lenders who modify loans from lawsuits rather than requiring modifications, treats bank employees more leniently than independent brokers, and offers distressed homeowners counseling instead of direct relief. On balance it is a genuine consumer protection bill with industry accommodations built in.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2008 and referred to four House committees, it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Spencer Bachus (R-AL) introduced the bill on April 22, 2008, with 31 original cosponsors, and 60 Republicans in total cosponsored it [S3][S4].

The Speaker referred it to the Financial Services Committee plus the Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, and Judiciary Committees, a four-way referral that splits a bill's provisions among committees and makes consideration harder [S1].
The only further action in the record is a May 23, 2008 referral of part of the bill to the Armed Services Subcommittee on Military Personnel [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever taken in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Independent mortgage brokers avoided new licensing, testing, and background check requirements, and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac avoided the bill's capital mandates and enforcement regime. Homeowners facing foreclosure gained nothing from this bill, though its ideas resurfaced in other legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mortgage brokers and the housing enterprises

for.name: Rep. Spencer Bachus
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee (ranking member)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 22, 2008 and assembled Republican cosponsors for it

for.name: 60 of 202 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the House Republican leader John Boehner

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; the House instead advanced majority-written housing legislation during the 2008 crisis

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 60 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced in a House run by Democrats who were writing their own housing legislation that year.

industries.industry: Independent mortgage brokers and loan originators
industries.note: Brokers would face FBI background checks, licensing exams, continuing education, and public disciplinary tracking — costs the bill does not impose equally on bank employees. Consumers get a verifiable record of who is selling them a loan.

industries.industry: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (government-sponsored enterprises)
industries.note: The bill replaces their lightly-empowered regulator with a Federal Housing Finance Agency that can set capital levels, cap executive compensation, and force corrective action. Stronger oversight was aimed at protecting taxpayers and the mortgage market.
Bank employees only register rather than obtain full licenses, giving depositories a lighter compliance burden than independent brokers — a competitive advantage built into the bill.
New disclosure, escrow, and appraisal rules add compliance costs, but a safe harbor shields lenders from liability when they voluntarily modify loans, and CRA credit rewards modification practices.
A new HUD Office of Housing Counseling and $45 million a year in authorized grants would fund counseling for buyers, renters, and borrowers facing foreclosure.
They would move under the new agency's oversight with new capital and disclosure rules, while gaining merger and joint-activity flexibility.
